title: Why live recording beats studio gimmicks
summary: Live dates avoid gimmicks and retakes, but Atlantic dislikes them; the Showcase date recorded with the lights off.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: Yeah, sure. What about the advantages -- Norman Grans has been claiming for a long time that if he had his choice, he'd much rather record live, whether it's a concert or a club.
Because then they're forced to not use gimmicks.
They can only get what you're doing. And usually they do much better than what they would do with gimmicks.
And yet, relatively few of your albums were recorded live that I can remember. Was it that -- does it cost that much more? I would think it would cost less.
Yeah, right. No retakes and you don't have to pay for studio time or space.
Did you sometimes ask that a live
Maybe they want to be so sure that everything is just right, that they want to --
It never is. When they come out, the drums are too soft, --
-- and they're not (unintelligible) the score to get the balance of the instruments that are playing.

I remember the one of the two times we worked together on a recording, you did something that worked out very effectively. It was the band that was -- they were just going to end, they'd been playing at the Showcase. And you said, turn the lights down. I think we turned them all the way off.
And then you began to make announcements as if it were in a club. And somehow, it worked. Did you ever try anything like that in other sessions?
All that music was in our heads, anyway.
